screens.title: Introduction to OOP Principles and Classes
screens.narratorSegment: Object-Oriented Programming changes how you think about software. Instead of writing a list of actions, you define the things you work with — their data and what they can do. In Python we create classes as blueprints and then make objects from those blueprints. That makes code easier to read, extend, and reuse. For example, a Dog class can describe name, breed, and behaviors like barking; each specific dog is an object with its own name and tricks. In this lesson you will learn what classes and objects are, how to initialize instance state with the constructor method, why the conventional self parameter links methods to a specific object, and how class attributes differ from instance attributes. You will also see concrete code examples that create objects, call methods, and show how state is kept per instance. By the end, you should be able to define a simple class, instantiate objects, and explain why OOP helps model real systems. Consider how a blueprint and a manufactured item relate — which parts of that analogy map to attributes, methods, and constructors?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Introduction
Introduction to OOP Principles and Classes
Model data and behavior together to build modular, reusable code.
In this lesson

You will learn what a class is, how to create objects, why constructors exist, and how self connects methods to instances. Concrete examples use a Dog class and a Book class activity.

Why it matters

OOP helps manage complexity by grouping data and behavior together, which improves readability, reuse, and scalability for real-world systems like libraries, inventory, and simulations.

Explore Key Topics
Classes
Blueprints that define attributes and methods.
Instances
Concrete objects created from classes.
Constructors
Initialize object state when created.
Concept sketch
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Dog class example (visual)
A class defines shared and per-object data. Each object holds its own name and tricks list while sharing the species label.
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"

    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.name = name
        self.breed = breed
        self.tricks = []

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"
Quick takeaway
Think in terms of things and their capabilities. Classes structure that thinking and constructors give each thing its starting state.
Coming up
Next we'll break objectives into hands-on skills: define classes, use self correctly, create instances, and implement constructors with practical examples.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice and assessment. First, you will explain the core principles of Object-Oriented Programming and why modeling with objects helps manage complexity. That includes defining what a class and an object are and comparing data and behavior grouping to procedural organization. Second, you will define a class in Python with attributes and methods, including naming conventions and simple examples, so you can write small, reusable blueprints. Third, you will understand the purpose and usage of the self parameter; you will be able to explain how Python passes the instance to instance methods and why forgetting self produces errors. Finally, you will create instances from a class and interact with their attributes and methods, practicing with examples like a Dog class. Each objective maps to a competency milestone that verifies you can read, write, and explain these concepts. screens.title: What is Object-Oriented Programming?
screens.narratorSegment: Object-Oriented Programming is a way of organizing software around objects that combine data and behavior. Instead of thinking only about functions that do work, you think about the things you manipulate: their attributes describe state and their methods express behavior. An easy analogy is LEGO building: a class is the LEGO mold or blueprint, and each assembled LEGO model is an object with its own color, stickers, and configuration. In Python, most values are already objects, but classes let you define custom objects that match your domain concepts. This approach supports modularity: each object is a self-contained unit, making it simpler to reason about and maintain code. It also promotes reusability because you can instantiate the same class many times and extend it later. A common misconception is that OOP always requires inheritance; in reality, starting with simple classes and clear responsibilities is usually the best path. Try to name the entities in a problem you know well — such as Student, BankAccount, or Sensor — and imagine which attributes and behaviors they should encapsulate. How would you map a physical object's properties into attributes and its actions into methods?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is OOP?
Definition and analogy
Think of classes as blueprints and objects as built things.
Definition
Objects combine state and behavior. A class is a template for creating such objects in Python, where attributes represent data and methods represent actions.
Analogy
A LEGO mold produces many similar blocks; a class produces many similar objects, each configured with its own pieces and stickers.
Common misconception
OOP is not only about inheritance. Many problems are solved with simple classes and composition; inheritance is one tool among several.
Concrete example — Dog class
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"

    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.name = name
        self.breed = breed
        self.tricks = []

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"
This example shows class attributes, instance attributes initialized in the constructor, and a simple method that uses instance state.
Key takeaway
Model the things you care about; keep related data and behavior together for clarity and reuse.

screens.title: Benefits of Using OOP
screens.narratorSegment: Adopting OOP gives practical benefits that matter when projects grow. First, modularity: classes let you break a program into smaller units that encapsulate state and behavior. A well-designed class hides its internal details and exposes a simple interface, making debugging and maintenance easier. Second, reusability: a class can be instantiated many times and reused across different parts of an application. You can also extend behavior through inheritance or composition, avoiding repeated code. Third, flexibility and scalability: when behavior changes, updating a single class implementation propagates to all instances, reducing risk and duplication. Fourth, intuitive modeling: mapping real-world entities like Student or BankAccount to classes helps stakeholders understand the code because the structure mirrors domain ideas. A typical misconception is that OOP always slows performance; while there is minimal overhead, the architectural benefits usually outweigh it for maintainability. Practice by identifying three entities in a small app and sketching classes for each. Which benefit would matter most as your app grows? Benefits of Using OOP means it structures code into maintainable, reusable pieces and maps programs to real-world domains.. In practical terms, modularity, reusability, flexibility, and intuitive modeling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Benefits of OOP
OOP benefits explained
Four practical advantages to guide design choices
Modularity
Encapsulate related state and behavior so each class is easier to test and maintain.
Reusability
Instantiate classes or extend them rather than copying logic across the codebase.
Flexibility & Scale
Centralized changes in classes reduce the surface area when features evolve.
Intuitive Modeling
Classes map closely to domain concepts, making designs easier to reason about.
Example scenario
A Car manufacturing system might model Car, Engine, and Factory as classes. Changes to Engine behavior are localized and tested within Engine methods.
Misconception
OOP is not a silver bullet; choose simple classes and avoid over-designing with excessive inheritance.
Key takeaway
Pick OOP when grouping state and behaviors yields clearer, reusable code that models real entities.

screens.title: Classes vs. Objects
screens.narratorSegment: A class and an object are related but distinct ideas. A class is a template that defines a set of attributes and methods that its objects will have. An object, or instance, is a concrete realization of that template with its own attribute values. For example, the Dog class defines name, breed, and tricks; Buddy and Lucy are individual Dog objects with different names and possibly different lists of tricks. Class attributes, like species in the Dog example, describe properties shared across all instances and are typically defined directly in the class body. Instance attributes are created for each object, usually in the constructor, so each object maintains its own state. A common confusion is expecting that changing a class attribute on one object will change it only for that object; in fact, class attributes are shared across all instances unless shadowed by an instance attribute. When designing, ask whether a value belongs to every instance equally or whether it will vary per object. That question helps decide class vs instance scope. Classes vs. Objects means classes define structure; instances hold unique state. class attributes are shared, instance attributes are per-object.. In practical terms, blueprints compared to concrete instances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Classes vs Objects
Classes and Instances
Understand shared vs. per-object state
Class (blueprint)
Defines attributes and methods that objects will have. Example: Dog defines breed and bark behavior.
Object (instance)
A concrete entity created from the class. Example: buddy is a Dog with a specific name and tricks.
Code example
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"  # class attribute

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name            # instance attribute

buddy = Dog("Buddy")
print(Dog.species)  # shared
print(buddy.name)   # per-instance
Key takeaway
Decide if a value is shared or unique, then place it at class or instance level accordingly.

screens.title: Anatomy of a Python Class
screens.narratorSegment: A Python class typically contains three parts: class attributes, the constructor method, and instance methods. Class attributes appear in the class body and are shared across all instances. The constructor, init, is a special method automatically called when you create an object; its job is to initialize instance attributes. Instance methods are functions defined inside the class that operate on instance data via the self parameter. For example, in a Dog class, species might be a class attribute, while name and tricks are initialized per-instance in init. Methods like bark and learn_trick reference self to read or modify that instance's attributes. When designing, list the pieces of state your objects need and then write methods that operate clearly on that state. A common design error is placing per-instance state at the class level, which causes unexpected sharing. Always test object creation to confirm attributes are distinct for each object. What instance attributes will you include the next time you design a class? Anatomy of a Python Class means combine class attributes, a constructor to initialize instance attributes, and methods that operate via self.. In practical terms, attributes, methods, and the constructor laid out. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Anatomy of a Class
Class structure
Design attributes and methods intentionally
Class attributes
Shared across instances; useful for constants or values common to all objects.
Constructor (__init__)
Sets up per-instance state like name, breed, or a list for tricks.
Instance methods
Operate on instance data using the self parameter, implementing behavior like bark or display_status.
Example anatomy
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"   # class attribute

    def __init__(self, name, breed):  # constructor
        self.name = name              # instance attribute
        self.breed = breed
        self.tricks = []

    def bark(self):                  # instance method
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"
Key takeaway
Plan attributes first, then implement constructor and methods that operate on that state through self.

screens.title: Class Attributes vs Instance Attributes
screens.narratorSegment: Class attributes are values set on the class object and shared by every instance. Instance attributes are set per object, usually inside the constructor, and they keep each object's unique state. In the Dog example, species is a class attribute because every dog here shares a biological label, while name and tricks are instance attributes because each dog has its own name and list. Access patterns differ: you can read a class attribute via the class or an instance, but modifying a class attribute on the class affects all instances that rely on it. A frequent learner error is placing mutable default values at the class level when you meant each instance to have its own list; instead, initialize mutable collections inside init so each instance gets a new collection. To decide where to place a value, ask: will this attribute be the same for every object of this class, or will it vary? That rule gives a clear design guideline. Class Attributes vs Instance Attributes means use class attributes for shared constants and instance attributes for per-object state, especially mutable data.. In practical terms, shared state versus per-object state and how to choose. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Class vs Instance Attributes
Class attribute vs instance attribute
Choose scope carefully to avoid shared-state bugs
Class attribute
Defined in class body. Shared across instances. Good for constants or values common to all objects.
Instance attribute
Created in __init__ via self. Unique to each instance. Required for per-object state, especially mutable collections.
Illustration
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"  # class attribute

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name             # instance attribute
        self.tricks = []             # instance-level mutable list
If tricks were defined at class level, all dogs would share the same list.
Common mistake
Defining mutable attributes at the class level causes unexpected sharing between instances. Initialize such attributes inside __init__ instead.

screens.title: The Constructor: __init__
screens.narratorSegment: The constructor method, named init in Python, is automatically called when you create a new object from a class. Its main purpose is to initialize the instance's attributes so each object starts in a well-defined state. Inside init you usually accept parameters needed to set up the object and assign them to self attributes. For example, when creating a Dog object you might pass name and breed, and inside init you set self. name and self. breed. Constructors can also prepare empty collections or default flags, such as setting a tricks list to an empty list or marking is_checked_out as False for a Book object. A typical mistake is forgetting required constructor parameters when instantiating, which raises a TypeError; another is placing per-instance mutable defaults at the class level rather than inside init. Use constructors to enforce invariants and make objects predictable from the moment they are created. How will you design your next object's constructor to make misuse harder? The Constructor: __init__ means constructors initialize object state and make each instance predictable and independent.. In practical terms, how object state is created and why constructors matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › The Constructor
__init__ explained
Initialize instance attributes reliably
Role of __init__
Set up per-instance state, validate inputs if needed, and provide sensible defaults like empty lists or False flags.
Good practice
Accept required parameters explicitly and initialize complex defaults within __init__ to avoid shared state.
Avoid
Don't use mutable objects as class-level defaults when they should be instance-specific.
Example — Book initialization
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, author, isbn):
        self.title = title
        self.author = author
        self.isbn = isbn
        self.is_checked_out = False
This constructor ensures every Book starts with a False checked-out status.

screens.title: The self Parameter
screens.narratorSegment: In Python, self is a conventional name for the first parameter of instance methods. It refers to the specific object the method is called on, allowing methods to read and modify that instance's attributes. When you write def bark(self): and then call buddy. bark(), Python implicitly passes buddy as the first argument so inside the method self. name refers to buddy's name. Forgetting to include self in a method definition causes errors because Python still passes the instance implicitly but the method signature does not accept it. That's a frequent source of NameError or TypeError for beginners. Another misuse is trying to use self outside of instance methods — self only makes sense inside methods where Python supplies the instance. Remember: self is not a keyword but a strong convention. You could technically name it differently, but following the convention improves readability across teams. As you practice, intentionally read error messages to see when Python expected or got different numbers of arguments; that will guide you to a missing or misplaced self parameter. The self Parameter means self is the instance reference passed implicitly by python so methods can operate on that object's state.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Using self
Understanding self
A convention that links methods to their instance
How it works
When you call an instance method, Python passes the instance as the first argument. self names that parameter so methods access the instance's attributes and other methods.
Common error
Omitting self from a method definition leads to argument mismatch errors at call time.
Best practice
Always include self as the first parameter of instance methods and use that name for readability.
Example call mechanics
def bark(self):
    return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

# call: buddy.bark()  --> Python passes buddy as first argument
Reflection
If you see a missing argument error when calling a method, check whether self was omitted from the method definition.

Implementing Book
Constructor, state changes, and status display
Starter template
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, author, isbn):
        # Initialize attributes here
        pass

    def check_out(self):
        # Mark checked out and print confirmation
        pass

        # Print title, author, ISBN, and status

Implementation example
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, author, isbn):
        self.title = title
        self.author = author
        self.isbn = isbn
        self.is_checked_out = False

    def check_out(self):
        self.is_checked_out = True
        print(f"Checked out: {self.title}")

    def return_book(self):
        self.is_checked_out = False
        print(f"Returned: {self.title}")

    def display_status(self):
        status = "Checked out" if self.is_checked_out else "Available"
        print(f"{self.title} by {self.author} (ISBN: {self.isbn}) - {status}")
Use this example to test the activity and then modify messages to suit your needs.
Check your understanding
After running the example, ensure status flips on checkout and returns to available after return_book is called.

screens.title: Common Errors and How to Debug Them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often face a handful of repeatable errors when working with classes. One is omitting self in a method definition; Python still provides the instance on call, so the method signature mismatches and a TypeError or unexpected name error occurs. Another common issue is mismatching constructor parameters: if init expects arguments and you call the class without them, Python raises a TypeError about missing required positional arguments. A third is accidentally defining mutable attributes at the class level, causing all instances to share a single list or dictionary; the symptom is that changing the attribute on one object appears to change it on all objects. To debug, read the error messages carefully — they tell you whether Python expected fewer or more arguments or which name was not defined. Add small print statements or interactive checks: after creating two objects, print attributes to ensure independence. These techniques pinpoint whether the problem is with signature, self usage, or attribute scope. Which error message will you look for first when debugging? Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Common Mistakes
Common errors and fixes
Missing self
Symptom: TypeError because the method received the instance but the definition did not expect it. Fix by adding self as the first parameter.
Constructor mismatch
Symptom: TypeError about missing arguments. Fix by calling class with correct parameters or providing defaults in __init__.
Shared mutable state
Symptom: Lists or dicts appear shared across instances. Fix by initializing mutable attributes inside __init__.
Debugging pattern
Reproduce the issue with minimal code, inspect attributes on two instances, and read the error trace to find the problematic line.
Quick test
Create buddy and lucy, add a trick to buddy, then print both tricks lists to ensure separation of state.

fullNarratorScript:
Object-Oriented Programming changes how you think about software. Instead of writing a list of actions, you define the things you work with — their data and what they can do. In Python we create classes as blueprints and then make objects from those blueprints. That makes code easier to read, extend, and reuse. For example, a Dog class can describe name, breed, and behaviors like barking; each specific dog is an object with its own name and tricks. In this lesson you will learn what classes and objects are, how to initialize instance state with the constructor method, why the conventional self parameter links methods to a specific object, and how class attributes differ from instance attributes. You will also see concrete code examples that create objects, call methods, and show how state is kept per instance. By the end, you should be able to define a simple class, instantiate objects, and explain why OOP helps model real systems. Consider how a blueprint and a manufactured item relate — which parts of that analogy map to attributes, methods, and constructors?

These objectives focus your practice and assessment. First, you will explain the core principles of Object-Oriented Programming and why modeling with objects helps manage complexity. That includes defining what a class and an object are and comparing data and behavior grouping to procedural organization. Second, you will define a class in Python with attributes and methods, including naming conventions and simple examples, so you can write small, reusable blueprints. Third, you will understand the purpose and usage of the self parameter; you will be able to explain how Python passes the instance to instance methods and why forgetting self produces errors. Finally, you will create instances from a class and interact with their attributes and methods, practicing with examples like a Dog class. Each objective maps to a competency milestone that verifies you can read, write, and explain these concepts. Try phrasing each objective as a short task to practice: define, instantiate, call, and explain. Which objective will you practice first?

This second objectives page highlights additional practical skills and common pitfalls to verify. You should be able to implement the constructor method init to initialize instance attributes and explain its role as the object's setup routine. You will distinguish class attributes from instance attributes and describe when each is appropriate. You will identify common mistakes, like forgetting self in method definitions, and know how such errors lead to NameError or TypeError because the method does not receive the instance. Finally, you will test objects interactively: create two instances, mutate one instance's state, and observe that the other remains independent when attributes are defined per-instance. These skills help you avoid shared-state bugs and make classes reliable building blocks. Each card below points to a small practice you can run in a Python prompt to confirm competency. Which pitfall will you test first?

Object-Oriented Programming is a way of organizing software around objects that combine data and behavior. Instead of thinking only about functions that do work, you think about the things you manipulate: their attributes describe state and their methods express behavior. An easy analogy is LEGO building: a class is the LEGO mold or blueprint, and each assembled LEGO model is an object with its own color, stickers, and configuration. In Python, most values are already objects, but classes let you define custom objects that match your domain concepts. This approach supports modularity: each object is a self-contained unit, making it simpler to reason about and maintain code. It also promotes reusability because you can instantiate the same class many times and extend it later. A common misconception is that OOP always requires inheritance; in reality, starting with simple classes and clear responsibilities is usually the best path. Try to name the entities in a problem you know well — such as Student, BankAccount, or Sensor — and imagine which attributes and behaviors they should encapsulate. How would you map a physical object's properties into attributes and its actions into methods?

Adopting OOP gives practical benefits that matter when projects grow. First, modularity: classes let you break a program into smaller units that encapsulate state and behavior. A well-designed class hides its internal details and exposes a simple interface, making debugging and maintenance easier. Second, reusability: a class can be instantiated many times and reused across different parts of an application. You can also extend behavior through inheritance or composition, avoiding repeated code. Third, flexibility and scalability: when behavior changes, updating a single class implementation propagates to all instances, reducing risk and duplication. Fourth, intuitive modeling: mapping real-world entities like Student or BankAccount to classes helps stakeholders understand the code because the structure mirrors domain ideas. A typical misconception is that OOP always slows performance; while there is minimal overhead, the architectural benefits usually outweigh it for maintainability. Practice by identifying three entities in a small app and sketching classes for each. Which benefit would matter most as your app grows? Benefits of Using OOP means it structures code into maintainable, reusable pieces and maps programs to real-world domains.. In practical terms, modularity, reusability, flexibility, and intuitive modeling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A class and an object are related but distinct ideas. A class is a template that defines a set of attributes and methods that its objects will have. An object, or instance, is a concrete realization of that template with its own attribute values. For example, the Dog class defines name, breed, and tricks; Buddy and Lucy are individual Dog objects with different names and possibly different lists of tricks. Class attributes, like species in the Dog example, describe properties shared across all instances and are typically defined directly in the class body. Instance attributes are created for each object, usually in the constructor, so each object maintains its own state. A common confusion is expecting that changing a class attribute on one object will change it only for that object; in fact, class attributes are shared across all instances unless shadowed by an instance attribute. When designing, ask whether a value belongs to every instance equally or whether it will vary per object. That question helps decide class vs instance scope. Classes vs. Objects means classes define structure; instances hold unique state. class attributes are shared, instance attributes are per-object.. In practical terms, blueprints compared to concrete instances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Python class typically contains three parts: class attributes, the constructor method, and instance methods. Class attributes appear in the class body and are shared across all instances. The constructor, init, is a special method automatically called when you create an object; its job is to initialize instance attributes. Instance methods are functions defined inside the class that operate on instance data via the self parameter. For example, in a Dog class, species might be a class attribute, while name and tricks are initialized per-instance in init. Methods like bark and learn_trick reference self to read or modify that instance's attributes. When designing, list the pieces of state your objects need and then write methods that operate clearly on that state. A common design error is placing per-instance state at the class level, which causes unexpected sharing. Always test object creation to confirm attributes are distinct for each object. What instance attributes will you include the next time you design a class? Class attributes are values set on the class object and shared by every instance. Instance attributes are set per object, usually inside the constructor, and they keep each object's unique state. In the Dog example, species is a class attribute because every dog here shares a biological label, while name and tricks are instance attributes because each dog has its own name and list. Access patterns differ: you can read a class attribute via the class or an instance, but modifying a class attribute on the class affects all instances that rely on it. A frequent learner error is placing mutable default values at the class level when you meant each instance to have its own list; instead, initialize mutable collections inside init so each instance gets a new collection. To decide where to place a value, ask: will this attribute be the same for every object of this class, or will it vary? That rule gives a clear design guideline. The constructor method, named init in Python, is automatically called when you create a new object from a class. Its main purpose is to initialize the instance's attributes so each object starts in a well-defined state. Inside init you usually accept parameters needed to set up the object and assign them to self attributes. For example, when creating a Dog object you might pass name and breed, and inside init you set self. name and self. breed. Constructors can also prepare empty collections or default flags, such as setting a tricks list to an empty list or marking is_checked_out as False for a Book object. A typical mistake is forgetting required constructor parameters when instantiating, which raises a TypeError; another is placing per-instance mutable defaults at the class level rather than inside init. In Python, self is a conventional name for the first parameter of instance methods. It refers to the specific object the method is called on, allowing methods to read and modify that instance's attributes. When you write def bark(self): and then call buddy. bark(), Python implicitly passes buddy as the first argument so inside the method self. name refers to buddy's name. Forgetting to include self in a method definition causes errors because Python still passes the instance implicitly but the method signature does not accept it. That's a frequent source of NameError or TypeError for beginners. Another misuse is trying to use self outside of instance methods — self only makes sense inside methods where Python supplies the instance. Remember: self is not a keyword but a strong convention. You could technically name it differently, but following the convention improves readability across teams. As you practice, intentionally read error messages to see when Python expected or got different numbers of arguments; that will guide you to a missing or misplaced self parameter. Beginners often face a handful of repeatable errors when working with classes. One is omitting self in a method definition; Python still provides the instance on call, so the method signature mismatches and a TypeError or unexpected name error occurs. Another common issue is mismatching constructor parameters: if init expects arguments and you call the class without them, Python raises a TypeError about missing required positional arguments. A third is accidentally defining mutable attributes at the class level, causing all instances to share a single list or dictionary; the symptom is that changing the attribute on one object appears to change it on all objects. To debug, read the error messages carefully — they tell you whether Python expected fewer or more arguments or which name was not defined.
